content: Researchers have discovered a way to kill leukemia cells by forcing them to remain highly active even as their energy supply is disrupted. The experimental treatment has produced promising results in mice and patient-derived cancer cells, including a particularly aggressive form of the disease that often resists treatment. The approach targets acute myeloid leukemia (AML), a rapidly progressing cancer of the blood and bone marrow that interferes with normal blood cell production. Developed by researchers at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden and Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, the treatment exploits the energy demands of malignant cells rather than directly attacking their DNA. At the center of the strategy is mTOR, a protein that helps regulate cell growth, metabolism, and activity. Under normal conditions, cells adjust these processes according to their available resources. The researchers designed a molecule called AcTor that blocks a signaling protein involved in controlling mTOR, allowing growth signals to remain active even when cellular energy production is impaired. AcTor was combined with ixazomib (IXZ), a drug used to inhibit cancer cell proliferation. Together, the treatments disrupt energy production in mitochondria while preventing leukemia cells from slowing their activity. Unable to balance their energy needs with their available resources, the cancer cells experience severe stress and die. The treatment emerged from a collaboration between biochemist Boaz Tirosh and computational chemist Leif Eriksson, whose expertise helped turn the underlying hypothesis into a potential drug. “Boaz Tirosh is a biochemist and understands the processes taking place within a cell. It was he who put forward the hypothesis for this treatment. I am a computational chemist and have designed a molecule that enters the cancerous cell and alters it in the way we want,” says Leif Eriksson, Professor of Physical Chemistry at the University of Gothenburg. In a study published in Molecular Cancer , the combination of AcTor and ixazomib demonstrated strong activity against AML in laboratory cell lines, primary samples from patients, and animal experiments. It also remained effective against TP53-mutant AML, an especially aggressive form of leukemia associated with poor outcomes and limited treatment options. The researchers found that the treatment eliminated malignant blood cells as well as leukemic stem cells. These stem cells can survive conventional therapies and regenerate the disease, contributing to relapse. The mouse experiments also suggested that the treatment could avoid the development of drug resistance, although this has not been established in patients. “It’s a completely new method and does not affect healthy blood cells; furthermore, our studies in mice show that drug resistance is avoided, which can otherwise happen,” says Leif Eriksson. The researchers also detected a biological response that might eventually help doctors assess whether the treatment is working. Cells exposed to the drug combination released a protein called ADM2, which could potentially serve as a measurable indicator of treatment activity. “We also observed that our treatment triggered the release of a protein (ADM2), which could therefore serve as a biomarker for the treatment’s response. This could guide future translational and clinical studies,” says Leif Eriksson. The findings remain preclinical, meaning that the combination has not yet been shown to be safe or effective in humans. Further studies will be needed to confirm its activity, evaluate potential side effects, and determine whether it can progress to clinical trials. Patients with relapsed or refractory AML, whose disease has returned or failed to respond to treatment, could be among those who might benefit if the approach eventually proves successful. Instead of relying primarily on treatments that damage cancer cell DNA, the research focuses on disrupting the metabolic processes that allow leukemia cells to survive. “Our study is an example of the shift toward focusing research on cancer metabolism within cells, rather than relying solely on methods that damage DNA. Drug development is very expensive, but we hope that our findings will generate sufficient interest to enable us to continue our research into a cure for this serious disease,” says Leif Eriksson. Reference: “AcTor, a novel mTOR stimulator, potentiates ixazomib for the treatment of acute myeloid leukemia” by Shakti P Pattanayak, Odai Darawshi, Omid Hajihassani, Jordan M Winter, Nicole Weiler, Melanie Ott, Florian Rothweiler, Jindrich Cinatl Jr., Martin Michaelis, Daniel J Lindner, Thomas D Green, Polina Krassovskaia, Raphael T Aruleba, Kelsey H Fisher-Wellman, Jason A Mears, David Wald, Leif A Eriksson and Boaz Tirosh, 27 May 2026, Molecular Cancer . content: Restoring blood flow to the brain seemed a promising way to protect thinking skills, but opening severely narrowed arteries did not deliver the cognitive boost researchers hoped for. A Columbia -led randomized trial found that people with severe carotid artery narrowing gained no additional cognitive benefit from stenting or surgery compared with medication alone over one year. The findings challenge the idea that reopening these arteries can reverse cognitive decline in patients without associated symptoms. “We had hoped that improving blood flow in the brain in this way would improve cognition—and there were tantalizing clues from animal studies and case series that it would,” says study leader Randolph Marshall, MD, the Elisabeth K. Harris Professor of Neurology at Columbia University Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons. “But when we put it to the test in a randomized clinical trial, comparing cognition after opening the blockage or treatment with medication alone, we did not see a difference.” The carotid arteries run through the neck and supply blood to the brain. Severe narrowing, known as carotid stenosis, is associated with cognitive impairment even in people who have never had a stroke. The link is particularly apparent when blood flow to the brain is reduced. That connection raised a compelling possibility: restoring circulation might help preserve or improve cognition. Stenting holds a narrowed artery open, while surgery removes the material causing the blockage. “We’ve thought for a long time that improving cognition by restoring blood flow with stenting or surgery could improve cognition, but until our study, the hypothesis had never been tested in a randomized clinical trial.” To investigate, the researchers enrolled 291 patients in CREST-H, all with carotid artery narrowing of at least 70% but no associated symptoms. They assessed brain blood flow and cognition at enrollment and again one year later. Cognitive scores improved slightly in both groups, but patients who underwent a procedure did no better than those treated with medication alone. CREST-H was part of CREST-2, a larger multicenter trial that Marshall helped design to compare approaches to preventing strokes in people with severe carotid blockages. In that trial, adding stenting to medication cut strokes by about half compared with medication alone. Surgery to remove the blockage did not show the same benefit. “Those results do appear to have changed practice already, and more of these patients are getting stents,” says Marshall. The cognitive findings, however, suggest that patients should not expect the procedure to improve their thinking skills beyond what medication alone provides. “We concluded that revascularization to reverse cognitive decline in these patients cannot be expected. Therefore, we need to reinforce the importance of preventing carotid stenosis to avoid its consequences,” says Marshall. Reference: “Revascularization in Asymptomatic Carotid Artery Stenosis With Hemodynamic Impairment and Cognitive Outcomes: The CREST-H Substudy of the CREST-2 Randomized Clinical Trial” by Randolph S. Marshall, Ronald M. Lazar, James F. Meschia, John Huston, Lloyd J. Edwards, Thomas G. Brott, Brajesh K. Lal, George Howard, Carlos Mena-Hurtado, Donald Heck, Navdeep Sangha, Giuseppe Lanzino, Vikram S. Kashyap, Herbert D. Aronow, Mel Sharafuddin, Jenifer Voeks, Yu Zhang, Kevin Slane and David S. Liebeskind, , JAMA . DOI: 10.1001/jama.2026.13384 This study is supported by the NIH (R01NS097876). The CREST-2 parent trials are supported by the NIH (U01NS080168, U01NS080165, and U01NS086872), the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, and the Department of Health and Human Services. content: A clinical trial has uncovered a molecular change in skeletal muscle that may help explain why exercise improves insulin sensitivity in people with Type 2 diabetes. A protein found in unusually high amounts in the muscles of people with Type 2 diabetes may be interfering with the body’s ability to respond to insulin. Researchers discovered that removing the protein, known as Miro1, restored insulin responsiveness in preclinical models, suggesting a possible new approach to treating insulin resistance. The study, published in Nature Communications , also found that aerobic exercise reduced Miro1 levels in people with Type 2 diabetes. Those reductions occurred alongside improvements in insulin sensitivity and the muscles’ ability to produce energy. Miro1 (Mitochondrial Rho GTPase1) sits on the outer membrane of mitochondria, the structures responsible for producing much of a cell’s usable energy. Skeletal muscle plays a major role in regulating blood sugar because it absorbs glucose from the bloodstream in response to insulin. When muscle becomes resistant to insulin, glucose is less effectively removed from the blood, contributing to the elevated blood sugar associated with Type 2 diabetes. To investigate Miro1’s involvement, scientists examined its effects in cells, preclinical models, and people with Type 2 diabetes. Their experiments showed that excess Miro1 impaired insulin responses in muscle, while removing the protein reversed those effects in preclinical models. “Insulin resistance in muscle is at the heart of Type 2 diabetes, and its molecular causes have remained frustratingly unclear. This study, the product of years of work, identifies Miro1 as a key part of the answer. By tracing Miro1 from cells to preclinical models to patients, we show that Miro1 accumulation impairs the muscle’s response to insulin, that removing it causally restores that response in our models, and that exercise reverses its buildup in people. For the field, this is a new therapeutic target. For patients, it deepens our understanding of why exercise is so effective and opens a path toward treatments that could one day complement it,” said senior author Dr. John P. Kirwan. The researchers also conducted a randomized controlled trial involving participants with obesity and Type 2 diabetes. One group performed aerobic exercise, while another received standard medical care. Participants assigned to exercise showed lower Miro1 levels in their muscles, together with improved insulin sensitivity and mitochondrial energy production. These human findings support a connection between exercise, Miro1, and metabolic health. However, they do not establish that reducing Miro1 is responsible for the benefits of exercise. The preclinical experiments provide more direct evidence that the protein can influence insulin responses. Kirwan led the research while working at LSU’s Pennington Biomedical Research Center. He has since been appointed executive director of the OU Health Harold Hamm Diabetes Center at the University of Oklahoma, where he will continue investigating the biological mechanisms of diabetes and potential treatments. The study’s first author, Elizabeth Heintz, conducted research as a doctoral candidate in Pennington Biomedical’s Integrated Physiology and Molecular Medicine Laboratory. Co-corresponding author Christopher Axelrod has since joined Kirwan at the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center. “This research exemplifies the breadth of scientific discovery at Pennington Biomedical, where research spans all levels, from basic science that reveals the biological mechanisms underlying disease to clinical studies and population-based research that informs public health,” said Dr. Jennifer Rood, Interim Senior Vice Chancellor and Executive Director of Pennington Biomedical. “Dr. Kirwan and his team’s findings on Miro1 demonstrate the value of this integrated approach, connecting fundamental discoveries about muscle function with insights into insulin resistance and the benefits of exercise in people with Type 2 diabetes. This work is advancing our understanding of diabetes and helping lay the foundation for future approaches to prevention and treatment.” Although removing Miro1 improved insulin responses in experimental models, researchers have not yet established whether targeting the protein would be safe or effective as a treatment for people. Further studies will need to clarify how Miro1 contributes to insulin resistance and whether modifying its activity can improve blood sugar regulation. At the Harold Hamm Diabetes Center, Kirwan plans to build on these findings through research that connects laboratory discoveries with studies involving people with diabetes. “Type 2 diabetes is an affliction in Oklahoma and nationally,” he said. “Ultimately, we are looking for cures, and we hope these recent findings could be part of the solution.” Reference: “Miro1 mediates skeletal muscle insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes” by Elizabeth C. Heintz, Wagner S. Dantas, Analisa L. Taylor, Elizabeth R. M. Zunica, Kathryn P. Belmont, Jackson M. Slone, Jacob T. Mey, Robbie Beyl, Bolormaa Vandanmagsar, Hailey A. Parry, Peter Ajayi, Brian Glancy, Christopher L. Axelrod and John P. Kirwan, 19 October 2026, Nature Communications . DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-77278-6 The research was supported by the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, the National Institute on Aging, the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health, the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute, and the National Institute of General Medical Sciences.
